corner_table_caption: Process, temperature and supply points simulated for the transimpedance stage. The typical point is the Monte Carlo process section evaluated with zero statistical offset at the \SI{37}{\celsius} on-body operating temperature; the four skew corners are the imported foundry corners, which carry \SI{25}{\celsius}. This run is corners only --- no Monte Carlo sampling was performed, so no mismatch or yield figures appear in this section.

figures.caption: Transimpedance $|Z_t| = |V_{\mathrm{OUT}}/I_{\mathrm{WE}}|$ of the closed transimpedance stage against frequency, over the five process corners, at the maximum gain setting ($R_f = \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}$) with \SI{1}{\micro\farad} of double-layer capacitance at the working electrode. The response is flat at \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm} to about \SI{200}{\hertz}, then peaks to \SIrange{1.00}{1.17}{\mega\ohm} near \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} before rolling off. That peak is a marginally stable loop rather than a design intent, and it is caused by the electrode capacitance and not by the amplifier: $C_{\mathrm{dl}}$ rolls the feedback factor off from \SI{0.28}{\hertz}, so the loop closes at roughly \SI{40}{\decibel} per decade.

Output voltage against the swept test-source current, over the five process corners. Conditions are $R_f = \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}$ with the working electrode held at $v_{\mathrm{cm}} = \SI{1.25}{\volt}$. The bench source draws its current \emph{out} of the WE node, so $i_{\mathrm{we}} = -I_{\mathrm{WE}}$ against the convention of Equation~(\ref{eq:tia-transfer}) and the plotted slope is $+R_f$: the amplifier sources this current through $R_f$ and the output rises. The \SI{\pm 2.26}{\micro\ampere} sweep takes the output to within \SI{12}{\milli\volt} of \texttt{vdd} and \SI{1.2}{\milli\volt} of \texttt{vss}. The corners overlay to the line width because the slope is the feedback resistor, an ideal component in this bench.

Error between the working-electrode potential and $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ across the same sweep --- the quality of the virtual ground the electrode sees. It stays inside \SI{\pm 0.4}{\milli\volt} over the full current range in both directions, and its slope is the input impedance of the stage, set by the loop gain available at the summing node. Against a \SI{1.25}{\volt} full-scale output this is under \SI{0.04}{\percent} of full scale, so the virtual ground is not an accuracy limit at this gain setting.

Open-loop gain of the transimpedance amplifier over the five process corners, by \texttt{stb} analysis through the feedback probe with the amplifier in unity feedback and a \SI{5}{\pico\farad} load. Miller compensation places the dominant pole near \SI{200}{\hertz} and gives a single-pole roll-off to a \SIrange{6.2}{7.6}{\mega\hertz} crossover; the corners overlay to within \SI{1.7}{\decibel} of DC gain. This is the amplifier's own response. The loop that closes around the electrode is a different loop, and it is not this well behaved --- see Figure~\ref{fig:tia-zt}.

Output voltage of the amplifier in unity feedback as a DC load current is drawn from its output, over the five process corners. Positive current is drawn out of the output node, so the amplifier must source it; the collapse at \SIrange{13.6}{15.6}{\micro\ampere} is the class-A second stage running out of the fixed current in M5. In the sinking direction the output holds within \SI{0.8}{\milli\volt} of $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ all the way to the \SI{-40}{\micro\ampere} end of the sweep, so the sinking capability is bounded below by the sweep and not measured.

Large-signal response with the amplifier open-loop, driven by a rail-to-rail input pulse into \SI{5}{\pico\farad}, over the five process corners. The falling edge is \num{1.7} times faster than the rising edge for the same reason the drive is asymmetric: the second stage is class~A, and M12 sinks the load with a device eight times wider than the fixed current source M5 that has to source it.

Rising edge of a \SI{1}{\volt} step ($v_{\mathrm{cm}} \pm \SI{0.5}{\volt}$) in unity feedback into \SI{5}{\pico\farad}, over the five process corners. The window is \SI{3.5}{\micro\second} around the edge at \SI{100}{\micro\second}; the falling edge at \SI{1.1}{\milli\second} is outside it. The output slews for about \SI{0.4}{\micro\second}, overshoots once by \SIrange{5.0}{9.0}{\percent} of the step and recovers without ringing --- the excursion is slew recovery, not small-signal ringing, which is what the \SI{88}{\degree} phase margin of Table~\ref{tab:tia-amp} predicts.

tables.caption: Closed-loop transimpedance figures by corner, from \texttt{TiaFbTB} at $R_f = \SI{560}{\kilo\ohm}$ with $C_{\mathrm{dl}} = \SI{1}{\micro\farad}$. Transimpedance at \SI{1}{\hertz} is within \SI{0.02}{\percent} of $R_f$ at every corner, so DC accuracy is set by the feedback resistor and not by the amplifier. The \SI{-3}{\decibel} bandwidth is not a usable signal bandwidth here because the peak lies inside it; the peaking rows are the ones that matter, and the two slow-NMOS corners are the worst at \SIrange{6.3}{6.4}{\decibel}.

DC transfer of the transimpedance stage by corner. The incremental gain falls by \SI{0.09}{\percent} between zero current and \SI{+2}{\micro\ampere}; that is the amplifier's finite loop gain, not resistor non-linearity, because $R_f$ is an ideal resistor in this bench. Virtual-ground error stays under \SI{0.4}{\milli\volt} in both directions. The supply current is the amplifier's own --- the feedback resistor, the load and the sources in this bench are ideal, so no electrode or ADC loading is included.

Small-signal figures of the amplifier alone, from \texttt{UnityFeedbackTB} with a \SI{5}{\pico\farad} load. A phase margin of \SIrange{87.6}{88.0}{\degree} with \SIrange{24}{26}{\decibel} of gain margin means the amplifier is heavily overcompensated for this load, which is why the step response of Table~\ref{tab:tia-step} does not ring. Neither number describes the transimpedance loop, whose feedback network includes the electrode capacitance; that loop is characterised in Table~\ref{tab:tia-closedloop}.

Input-referred noise of the amplifier, from \texttt{UnityFeedbackTB}, where the noise gain is unity. The spectrum is flicker-dominated across the whole signal band --- an \num{11}-fold fall from \SI{10}{\hertz} to \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} --- so the integrated figure is set by the input pair's area rather than by its bias current. \textbf{This is not the noise of the transimpedance stage:} the electrode capacitance raises the noise gain from unity at DC in proportion to $2\pi f R_f C_{\mathrm{dl}}$ above \SI{0.28}{\hertz}, so the closed-loop output noise is considerably larger. It was not simulated in this run.

Output drive limits by corner, from \texttt{DriveTB} with a \SI{5}{\pico\farad} load. The sourcing limit is the current at which the output has drooped \SI{1}{\percent} (\SI{12.5}{\milli\volt}) below $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$. Sinking is not resolved: the output is still within \SI{0.8}{\milli\volt} of $v_{\mathrm{cm}}$ at the \SI{-40}{\micro\ampere} end of the sweep, so \SI{40}{\micro\ampere} is a lower bound rather than a measurement. The consequence for the minimum-gain setting is discussed above.

Slew rate in each direction, taken as the extreme of the numerical derivative of the open-loop rail-to-rail transient of Figure~\ref{fig:tia-slew}. These are open-loop full-swing values into \SI{5}{\pico\farad} and are not closed-loop settling rates.

Step response by corner, from \texttt{StepUnityFeedbackTB}: a \SI{1}{\volt} step into \SI{5}{\pico\farad}, with overshoot expressed as a percentage of the step. The single overshoot peaks about \SI{0.55}{\micro\second} after the edge and is gone immediately: the residual error \SI{1}{\micro\second} after the edge is already \SI{0.02}{\percent} of the step. The falling edge, driven by the strong NMOS M12 rather than by the current source M5, shows essentially none.

Input offset, and the input--output range over which the unity-gain follower tracks its input to better than \SI{2}{\milli\volt}. The PMOS input pair puts the lower edge within \SI{5}{\milli\volt} of \texttt{vss}, which is what a stage holding a working electrode near ground needs; the upper edge is \SIrange{2.03}{2.07}{\volt}, about \SI{0.44}{\volt} short of the supply. Offset is under \SI{0.2}{\milli\volt} at every corner, but offset is a mismatch quantity and this is a corner run --- it is not characterised until a Monte Carlo run exists.
